concept.name: Theta
concept.definition: Theta is the sensitivity of an option's price to the passage of time, holding all other inputs constant — conventionally reported as the (typically negative) change in option value per day. Long options usually have negative theta and short options positive theta; theta is largest in magnitude for at-the-money options near expiration.
concept.intuition: Theta is the daily rent you pay to own an option: every day that passes with the stock unmoved, a little more of the premium evaporates.
concept.mechanics: Theta = -dV/d(tau) by practitioner convention, where tau is time to expiry. Time decay is non-linear, accelerating into expiration for ATM options, and it is the mirror image of gamma: long-gamma positions pay theta and short-gamma positions collect it. Deep ITM European puts can have positive theta because of discounting effects.
concept.failure_modes: Theta is a model value assuming constant implied volatility and price — real decay is lumpy (weekends, events, IV changes), so daily theta estimates routinely misstate actual overnight P&L. Strategies sold as 'theta harvesting' silently assume realized volatility stays below implied.
concept.misconceptions: Theta is not guaranteed income for sellers: it is compensation for bearing gamma risk, and the two are linked by the pricing PDE. Buyers likewise do not 'lose theta' on weekends in a simple daily pro-rata way — models price decay continuously while markets price it in discrete jumps.
concept.example: A $100-strike call trading at $3.00 with theta -0.05 loses about $0.05 overnight if price and implied volatility are unchanged; after a quiet week it would be worth roughly $2.65, all else equal.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OCC) — Understanding Options Greeks
